abstract: This session discusses enforcement of the EMC controls in the UK. The change to the EMC Directive and consequently the UK implementing regulations comes at an interesting time for Trading Standards officers. The current mantra from Government, through its Better Regulation Initiative, is that Trading Standards officers should adopt a light touch enforcement style and ensure that business is not overly burdened by bureaucratic red tape. The goal is an environment where inspection is performed according to risk, regulatory requirements are clear and compliance is easy: An approach most Trading Standards services already employ. In contrast, the new regulations, while extending the process of self-certification will introduce more meticulous documentation requirements. In the case of Fixed Installations, the means of achieving and demonstrating compliance presents an interesting test. In general, the Business community continues to look for visible enforcement of the EMC rules, yet with local government in a funding crisis and existing central government funding mechanisms that do not allow targeted funding, trading standards services are struggling to fulfil their statutory duties. Consequently, given the lack of complaints of unfair competition, market surveillance is infrequent, the existing regime is becoming inadequate, and change is needed. Without change, market surveillance will consist of well meaning officers investigating complaints that they do not understand and may not have the capacity to rectify regulatory breaches. That cannot be acceptable to anyone, but the rogue. The challenge for trading standards officers is to meet these demands and ensure that the EMC legislation is applied sensibly and that compliance is achieved without having to resort to legal action.

articleTitle: General Principles on the EMC of Large Systems and Installations for Designers
publicationTitle: 2007 IET Seminar on New Regulatory Requirements and Techniques for Achieving Electromagnetic Compatibility in Commercial Buildings
abstract: There are significant changes in the new EMC Directive 2004/108/EC with regard to the compliance of installations with essential requirements. The presentation covers the impact of the new EMC Directive on building development and the issues that need to be addressed to ensure that both legal and contractual requirements are achieved. In many cases it is important to define, or measure, the electromagnetic environment so that key aspects are addressed and the effective building design principles for EMC are determined. Installed equipment should be supplied only when compliant with applicable standards but often there is a requirement to determine whether the standards are sufficient and whether there are additional issues that need to be addressed. Generally application of Codes of Practice for installation design and construction will ensure that good engineering practice is applied, an essential issue under the new directive.

articleTitle: EMC for Installations - Practical Design and Assessment Methods
publicationTitle: 2007 IET Seminar on New Regulatory Requirements and Techniques for Achieving Electromagnetic Compatibility in Commercial Buildings
abstract: At a truly practical level, documentation control and good engineering practice are the minimum elements required to meet the EMC protection requirements for fixed installations. This presentation attempts to illustrate some best practice principles for design, some EMC mitigation methods and highlight EM assessment techniques which could be employed. The topics covered by this presentation include: (i) Cable routing and installation; (ii) Earthing and bonding; (iii) Lightning protection; (iv) Power system installation and quality; (v) EMC mitigation methods; and (vi) Assessment methods.

articleTitle: EMC for Sound and TV Installations
publicationTitle: 2007 IET Seminar on New Regulatory Requirements and Techniques for Achieving Electromagnetic Compatibility in Commercial Buildings
abstract: EMC compliance for a system is largely about managing the cable design. The most disruptive interference sources are always devices that are not designed to transmit anything, and tend to be part of the overall system design. EMI is distributed by cable structures, so the main job is to identify coupling paths and develop techniques to minimise the tendency of wires to become antennae.

articleTitle: Issues in the EMC Directive that Address Installations
publicationTitle: 2007 IET Seminar on New Regulatory Requirements and Techniques for Achieving Electromagnetic Compatibility in Commercial Buildings
abstract: Commercial buildings are fixed installations under the new EMC Directive 2004/108/EC, and the UK Regulations SI 2006 No. 3418 that implement it. This paper describes the requirements in the new legislation that affect fixed installations from 20 July this year. There are new responsibilities placed on those responsible for fixed installations, and in some cases relaxed requirements for apparatus that comprises them. The responsibilities and documentation requirements placed on manufacturers, owners and users will be described, and guidance on how to interpret these requirements and comply with them will be provided.

articleTitle: EMC Management Planning: Application to Commercial Buildings in Complex Electromagnetic Environments
publicationTitle: 2007 IET Seminar on New Regulatory Requirements and Techniques for Achieving Electromagnetic Compatibility in Commercial Buildings
abstract: Achieving EMC within the built environment should be viewed as having two elements, a technical element that is comprised of modelling and measurement, and a management plan element that packages the technical elements with management rules (risk analysis, relevant declarations of conformity, responsible person, etc). The application of a structured planning approach helps to ensure that a high operational state is achievable whilst controlling the costs of implementing EMC best practices during the design and construction stages. This presentation will cover the elements required to achieve effective EMC management planning for commercial buildings operating in complex electromagnetic environments as well as being able to demonstrate compliance with the EMC Directive.

publicationTitle: 2007 IET Seminar on New Regulatory Requirements and Techniques for Achieving Electromagnetic Compatibility in Commercial Buildings
abstract: To prevent interference to data transmission, data wiring must be run separately from mains wiring. EN 50174-2:2000 gives installation requirements for the separations required. In practice it can be difficult to achieve the mandated separations. This case study describes measurements made of compliant and non-compliant wiring over a 30kHz to 20MHz frequency range. On the basis of the measurements made of the compliant wiring it was found it was possible to recognise non- compliant wiring by measurement. Once it was possible to clearly distinguish between non- compliant and compliant wiring, remedial measures were made to bring the non-compliant wiring into compliance. The remedial measures will be described.

articleTitle: The Gap Analysis Approach to Compliance
publicationTitle: 2007 IET Seminar on New Regulatory Requirements and Techniques for Achieving Electromagnetic Compatibility in Commercial Buildings
abstract: From 20 July 2007 new requirements apply to new and existing fixed installations that are modified in a way that affect their EMC performance. Fixed installations must be installed applying good engineering practices which must be documented and retained by a "responsible person" for the fixed installation. In addition the responsible person must have a level of competence to be able to determine that the configuration of the installation complies with the essential requirements. This paper describes an approach to determining compliance that we have used successfully on many projects, using gap analysis and hazard identification techniques, which can be applied by the responsible person to his assessment of fixed installations.
